---
title: "Component 9 — Composite & Storytelling"
---

Four products that tie every measurement together: **Five-Tool Scoreboard**,
**Player of the Game**, **Rivalry Radar**, and **Prospect Spotlight**.

## Five-Tool Scoreboard

The problem with blending speed, power and arm is that they are measured in
different things — mph on the run, mph off the bat, mph on the throw. Averaging
them directly is meaningless.

The fix is to convert each tool to a **league percentile first**, then average.
That makes the blend honest, and it makes the output instantly legible: a 97
means *better than 97 % of the league*.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-fivetool
#| eval: false
source("../R/R09_composite.R")

five <- five_tool_scoreboard(burner, smash, cannons, min_tools = 2, top = 10)
five
plot_five_tool(five, player = "PHD-8007")
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-fivetool
#| eval: false
from components import c09_composite as c09
c09.five_tool_scoreboard(burner, smash, cannons, top=10)
```

:::

| player | speed pct | power pct | arm pct | tools | score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PHD-8007 | 98.6 | 98.1 | 97.8 | 3 | **98.2** |
| ANI-8572 | 94.9 | 99.4 | 99.2 | 3 | 97.8 |
| VAS-7028 | 98.3 | 99.4 | 94.3 | 3 | 97.3 |

::: {.callout-note}
`tools_measured` is reported alongside the score. A player with only two
measured tools is not silently flattered by having the third ignored — the
reader can see exactly what went into the number.
:::

## Player of the Game

Not a box-score line, but a **win-probability** line: who actually did the most
to win it. Batters are credited with their WPA; pitchers are credited with the
*negative* of the WPA they allowed.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-potg
#| eval: false
player_of_the_game(pbp, "y1_d122_IOL_VAS", top = 5)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-potg
#| eval: false
c09.player_of_the_game(enriched, "y1_d122_IOL_VAS", top=5)
```

:::

In the showcase game the engine's pick was the hitter who homered in the bottom
of the 11th — a single swing worth **+83 %** of win probability.

## Rivalry Radar

Team-vs-team tale of the tape, built entirely from tracking aggregates rather
than a traditional box score.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-rivalry
#| eval: false
rivalry_radar(pbp, "VAS", "IOL")
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-rivalry
#| eval: false
c09.rivalry_radar(enriched, tabs["hits"], tabs["sprints"], lu, "VAS", "IOL")
```

:::

Comparing average exit velocity, WPA per plate appearance and the count of
high-leverage trips gives a matchup preview that says something a standings
table cannot.

## Prospect Spotlight

One player's tool grades, in the shape a scoreboard animates: value, league
percentile, and a scouting-style grade.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| label: r-prospect
#| eval: false
prospect_spotlight("PHD-8007", burner, smash, cannons, baselines)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| label: py-prospect
#| eval: false
c09.prospect_spotlight("PHD-8007", burner, smash, cannons, baselines)
```

:::

| tool | value | percentile | grade |
|---|---|---|---|
| speed | 21.9 mph | 98.6 | ELITE |
| power | 124.8 mph | 98.1 | ELITE |
| arm | 96.5 mph | 97.8 | ELITE |

Grades follow the familiar scouting ladder — ELITE, PLUS-PLUS, PLUS, AVERAGE,
BELOW AVG — so the graphic reads the same way a scout's report does.

## Putting it on the screen

Every component in this book feeds one decision: **what goes on the big screen
right now?** The Highlight Score answers it by fusing game importance with
physical spectacle:

$$\text{HighlightScore} = 100 \times \frac{\sum_i w_i s_i}{\sum_i w_i}$$

Each component is mapped to a common 0–1 excitement scale before combining, so
mph, feet and probabilities can be weighed against each other honestly.
Measurements missing for a play are dropped and the weights renormalize — a play
is never penalized for lacking a sensor reading.

The validation that matters: the engine's highest-scoring moments of the season
are **walk-off home runs in extra innings and game-ending outs at leverage
4.8–8.2** — the same plays a human editor would choose, arrived at from tracking
data alone.
